newsitem.title: FRANCE: Commission to discuss ban on British gelatine exports.
newsitem.headline: Commission to discuss ban on British gelatine exports.

text.p: The European Commission will discuss next week steps to make it legally impossible to export British gelatine, though none is currently being exported, a Commission spokesman said on Wednesday.

The move is designed to reassure consumers who were scared off beef -- gelatine is a by-product widely used in food, cosmetics and medicine -- after the British government last year triggered a massive health scare by admitting there was a link between mad cow disease and a fatal human equivalent.

The spokesman said that EU Food Safety Commissioner Emma Bonino told the Commission that a multidisciplinary committee last week said there was no reliable process to ensure that gelatine was safe from mad cow disease, known medically as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).
"We want a legal cover for what is happening at the moment," said the spokesman.
British-sourced gelatine has not been exported since the commission last June controversially eased an export ban, subject to tough preconditions.
British manufacturers considered the heat processing terms were so stringent as to make production uneconomic. Instead they have been using beef raw materials from other countries.
Bonino earlier told reporters that there might also have to be a formal ban on the use of specified risk material from sheep and cattle -- skull, brain, eyes, spleen -- for manufacturing gelatine.
It would cover all EU countries and imports from third countries, she added.
"We will have to take action in the light of the new information presented but the end result will be rather positive, notably for the consumer," Bonino said.

Following next week's discussion, EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler will decide whether to draft a proposal for discussion by the EU's Standing Veterinary Committee of senior member state officials. A final decision could be taken by May 1.
The EU imposed a worldwide ban on British exports of beef and beef products in March 1996 shortly after London disclosed that BSE could be passed to humans.
The fatal cattle brain disease has killed more than 165,000 British cattle since the first case was reported 10 years ago, compared with fewer than 500 in other EU countries.
